Daniel’s core move—“BDI isn’t how I think, it’s how I explain myself”—is persuasive as a critique of *introspection-as-transparency*, but it quietly slides from “my access is limited” to “thinking is in principle uninterpretable.” Those are different claims. A lot of cognitive science suggests the first without committing to the second: people routinely confabulate reasons and misreport causes, yet their behavior remains statistically and functionally modelable at multiple levels (habits, heuristics, goal-directed control, etc.). Classic work on the gap between reported reasons and actual causal determinants is [Nisbett & Wilson (1977)](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1978-06664-001); it supports Daniel’s suspicion about self-explanation, but it doesn’t imply a “flat, wild” black box so much as *limited first-person observability plus many partial models*.

A sharper lineage for Daniel’s point is pragmatist/anti-realist about mental-state talk: beliefs and desires (and BDI-style states) can be treated as *interpretive instruments* for prediction and coordination rather than inner inventory. That’s close to Dennett’s “intentional stance,” where attributing beliefs/desires is a strategy that often works even if the underlying mechanism is messy or unknown ([Dennett, *The Intentional Stance*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Intentional_Stance)). It also echoes Wittgenstein’s pressure against private inner “read-outs”: what counts as “having a belief” is anchored in public criteria and use, not a special kind of introspective perception ([*Philosophical Investigations*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein/)). Read that way, Daniel’s “I only make it interpretable for inter-person understanding” isn’t a confession of epistemic failure; it’s an important claim about *what mental vocabulary is for*: not mirroring hidden mental objects, but enabling shared reason-giving, accountability, and planning.

One blind spot is that BDI is doing at least two jobs that Daniel conflates: (1) a *personal-level* vocabulary for giving reasons (where “artificial interpretability” may be exactly the point), and (2) an *engineering abstraction* in AI/cognitive modeling that doesn’t pretend to be phenomenology. If Daniel means “my lived cognition doesn’t come in propositional packets,” then traditions like enactivism and embodied cognition may fit; if he means “mental-state attribution is a socially learned interpretive practice,” Dennett/Wittgenstein are the cleaner ancestors. The post would gain clarity by specifying which target is in view: *introspective access*, *phenomenological texture*, or the *legitimacy of intentional-state models*—because the right “school of thought” depends on that distinction.
